title: Deep TMS for Schizophrenia?
subtitle: The good news for brain stimulation in psychotic illness keeps on coming, maybe.
body_html:
Although I’ve spent much of my career as a psychiatrist working with severe mood disorders (not to mention personality disorders), I thought I was going to be a schizophrenia researcher for the first three years of my training. Part of that has to do with the mentors you have—and between David Garrison, M.D., Stephen Geisler, M.D., Leo Lopez, M.D., John Kane, M.D., and Christoph Correll, M.D., I was surrounded by myriad docs who valued research and compassion in the healing of those with schizophrenia.

My very first published paper was on the topic of clozapine “re-challenge” (a.k.a. trying it again) after life-threatening side effects.

Thus, I couldn’t be more pleased to see the science I love—brain stimulation and neuromodulation—begin to make real strides in a population whose needs have always been close to my heart.

I’ve got a podcast on the topic, available here, and I’ve had a few articles in the recent past on the subject of treatment of psychosis with transcranial magnetic stimulation:

However, traditional TMS has some limitations: it’s very focal, targeting approximately one cubic centimeter of the brain at a time. This doesn’t allow for error-free placement of a coil or engagement of larger brain networks. Those who know me well know I’ve had a long relationship with BrainsWay and its H-coil systems (branded “Deep TMS”), which allow engagement of vast swaths of neurocircuitry all at once. I’ve even been a PI on their accelerated dTMS “SWIFT” trial, which led to FDA approval recently. Now, we have a new study on the use of deep TMS (dTMS) in schizophrenia.1

Deep Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation over the Anterior Cingulate Cortex in Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenia: A Pilot Double-blind, Randomized Controlled Trial

Deep TMS coils differ from figure-of-8 coils in size. The H7 coil (as used in this trial) is massive:

Different from the previously mentioned H-coils, the H7 coil is designed for targeting the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) (Harmelech et al., 2021). It achieves a subdural stimulation depth of 3cm with a volume of 40.3 cm3,

TMS is different than a drug—you can use it in different patterns of stimulation. For patients with depression, we are most often turning up the firing of neurons in a specific area of the brain. That pattern of stimulation isn’t the only possible pattern—we can turn down the firing of neurons in a durable way, too. There are both “on switch” and “off switch” variants of TMS!

In schizophrenia, some brain circuits are hyperexcitable. They fire too much! An effective treatment might cool things down a bit:

Recent evidence from Barone et al. (Barone et al., 2025) reported that patients with Treatment Resistant Schizophrenia (TRS) demonstrating the most pronounced cortical hyperexcitability and impaired plasticity. Some neuroimaging studies have found that ACC shows elevated glutamate levels and reduced GABA levels in antipsychotic non-responders compared with responders, observed in both first-episode2

As a brief reminder, glutamate stimulates neuronal firing, while GABA inhibits it. Too much glutamate? Too much brain activity in a circuit. Too little GABA? Same. I’m not a big fan of neurotransmitter-heavy explanations of brain disorders, but this evidence leads to the scientific rationale to try something a little radical—what if we treated patients with schizophrenia with the OPPOSITE of the treatment we use in OCD and Depression?

Share

Well, that “opposite” pattern of stimulation is what the authors did in this study.

Twenty-three patients with TRS were randomly allocated to receive either active or sham dTMS, undergoing 20 sessions of 1 Hz dTMS over 4 weeks.

The data analysis was not “clean” —they excluded patient who dropped out because they got worse:

Six participants who dropped out before the first post-baseline assessment (two consent withdrawals, four symptom aggravations) were excluded.

However, in those who concluded the pilot study:

The results indicated a significantly greater reduction in PANSS scores over time (F = 4.591, p = 0.018). Further analysis of symptom domains revealed that the dTMS intervention primarily ameliorated positive symptoms (F = 3.738, p = 0.037), with significant improvement compared to the sham at the end of treatment (difference = -4.306, 95 %CI [-6.961, -1.650]; p = 0.002).

But wait, what about those who dropped out?!? Well, I agree with you, dear readers. However, if you accept that a treatment that could be the opposite of antidepressant might make some people feel worse, and still be potentially biologically active? Well, then this pilot might be worth following up on.

Psychotic illnesses are challenging to live with, and our most vulnerable patient deserve more bold science such as this to discover what the full range of possible interventions might be.

Thanks for reading!

Psychiatry Res. 2025 Oct 1;353:116756. doi: 10.1016/j.psychres.2025.116756. Epub ahead of print. PMID: 41072338.
